2.7 Passive Rack Isolation System  
The Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS) hardware is installed on the CIR ISPR structure in 
order to passively isolate the rack from on-orbit vibrations.  The combination of integrated rack 
and PaRIS provides vibration isolation in both dynamic load path directions (i.e., attenuating 
vibrations imposed on the rack by the ISS vehicle as well as attenuating vibrations induced on 
the ISS vehicle by the rack, without consuming any ISS power, thermal, or data/command 
system resources.  It will attenuate vibratory accelerations above 1 Hz to the ISPR by suspending 
the ISPR from the International Space Station (ISS) module structure using passive dampers and 
springs.  The utility umbilical assembly provides a low bias force and spring rate connection 
between the module structure and the payload rack structure for utility pass through. 
 
The PaRIS is composed of the following: 
 
x Upper isolation strut adapter/interface assembly 
x Upper lock–down/snubbed assembly 
x Lower isolation adapter/interface assembly 
x Lower lock–down/snubbed assembly 
x Utility umbilical assemblies 
x Passive isolation units 
x Installation/adjustment/maintenance hardware 
 
PaRIS utilizes the spring / dampers to isolate the rack from the ISS module structure at 
frequencies above 0.5 Hz.  Unique utility cables and hoses are designated to all PaRIS 
applications.  The utility services have a service loop between the ISS vehicle interface and the 
PaRIS host rack to help in removing the force induced by them.  The utility umbilical assembly 
interfaces with the module at the Utility Interface Panel (UIP) connectors.  
2.8 Science Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) 
The Science Acceleration Measurement System (SAMS) is an ISS based system that collects 
acceleration data and distributes this data to the science community.  The distributed architecture 
of SAMS allows many sensors to be deployed at once, each independently collecting 
acceleration data and sending the data to a main control unit.  The control unit can handle 
different types of sensors collecting data at different rates at the same time.  The control unit then 
stores the data on its hard drive and sends the data to Payload Information Management System 
(PIMS) on the ground.  PIMS can then distribute the desired data to the user on the ground.  CIR 
includes a SAMS Tri-axial Sensor Head Ethernet stand alone (SAMS TSH-ES) sensor that 
extends this SAMS system into the rack. 
 
Users on the ground contact the PIMS or SAMS ground operations to have them issue 
commands or provide data.  Ground controllers issue commands to the sensor include starting 
acceleration data collection, changing the acceleration data’s frequency range, and stopping 
acceleration data collection.  Nominally, the CIR TSH begins data telemetry on rack power-up. 
The SAMS is mounted on the front of CIR Optics Bench allowing it to measure accelerations on 
a structure rigidly coupled the combustion chamber.

3.0 
CIR CONFIGURABLE CAPABILITIES AND RESOURCES 
The CIR provides a set of equipment that provides capabilities above those identified in the base 
configuration described in section 2.0.  This hardware is launched in a stowage configuration and 
installed by the flight crew as required to support a particular science investigation.  Consumable 
resources such as pressurized gas bottles, adsorber cartridges and I/O Processor hard disk drives 
are also included as configurable capabilities.  Much of this hardware is currently manifested on-
orbit and is available for use.  Hardware not currently on-orbit will need to be manifested 
3.1 Science Diagnostics Packages 
The CIR science diagnostics are complete avionics packages including software ready for 
installation and operation in the CIR.  These capabilities include illumination, imaging, image 
acquisition and processing.  A summary of capability and specification is provided in TABLE IV 
and 0  
The CIR specific Diagnostics Packages include: 
x Image Acquisition Modules (IAM) 
x Diagnostic Packages 
x High Bit Depth Multispectral Package (HiBMs) 
x Low Light Level Ultraviolet Package (LLL-UV) 
x Illumination Package.  
 
The Diagnostic Packages are mounted on the Optics Bench using common interfaces to permit 
movement of packages to various window locations for maximum science support flexibility.  
This approach emphasizes packaging modularity for operational flexibility and maintainability. 
Standardized optical interfaces (referred to as the flange mounts) are used between modules.  
These interfaces permit module arrangements to be reconfigured on orbit if required by science.

3.1.1 
Illumination Package 
The Illumination Package FIGURE 14 consists of a laser diode source and a collimating optical 
system, which is used to provide monochromatic illumination with a center wavelength between 
650 - 660nm. 
Two laser diodes are installed in the Illumination Package.  One is the primary laser diode and 
the second is included as a spare.  Both laser diodes are fiber coupled, each with its own FC/PC 
type fiber-optic connection at the Illumination Control Module (ICM), so the output from both 
cannot be used at the same time.  Each laser diode contains a photodiode to provide feedback of 
power output and a temperature transducer to monitor the diode temperature.  The laser diode is 
operated below the lasing threshold current and serves as a non-coherent illumination source.   
The Illumination Package can be used together with the HiBMs Package as a uniform 
illumination background source for soot absorption measurements in soot volume fraction 
applications, for shadowgraph measurements or for droplet diameter measurements.  The 
modular design supports future growth considerations.   
Illumination Package Specifications and Features:  
x 90 mm diameter CW beam 
x Collimation: 0.339° maximum divergence 
x 8-bit programmable output level (0-255) 
x Output power < 5 maw typical; used below lasing threshold current 
x 60% Illumination field uniformity 
x Peak Wavelength: between 650 and 660 nm 
x Spectral Bandwidth: < 10 nm maximum at 50% points 
 
Laser Diode Characteristics: 
x 300-350 maw max output power 
x Continuous Wave (CW) operation  
x Center Wavelength: 650-660 nm 
x Fiber Pigtailed; 0.22 Numerical Aperture 
3.1.2 
Low Light Level Packages 
The Low Light Level Ultra-Violet (LLL-UV) Package is based on a 1-megapixel digital, 
monochrome camera with a 1024x1024, frame transfer CCD array, providing 12 bit digital 
imaging capability.  The CCD is directly coupled to an 18 mm Gen-II-UV Micro-channel Plate 
Intensifier to provide maximum response at short wavelengths, including the OH emission line at 
310 nm.  The intensifier includes gating control that allows varied exposure times.  This function 
is used both to protect the Intensifier from overexposure and as a means to match the intensity of 
the event being viewed, such as a flame.  The package includes fast numerical aperture optics 
with high UV transmission characteristics and provision for spectral filtering of the transmitted 
illumination (Figure 14).  The LLL-UV Package is provided to produce images of events or 
objects at low radiance levels.  The LLL-UV Package can be positioned on the Optics Bench to

3.1.3 
High Bit-Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) Package  
The HiBMs Package is based on a telemetric imaging optical system and a high resolution 12-bit 
output digital camera.  The modular package is designed for operational flexibility.  The HiBMs 
Diagnostic Package consists of a spectral filter, or filter compensator glass, a Prism Module, a 
telemetric optical system, a fixed mirror module, a DCM, and a high resolution digital camera 
shown in FIGURE 15. 
 
FIGURE 15. HiBMS Package  
This diagnostic package has the capability of measuring two characteristics of soot producing 
flames: (1) the soot temperature field and (2) the soot volume fraction.  The soot temperature 
field is determined by measuring the percentage of laser illumination and the soot volume is 
measured from the Illumination Package that is absorbed by soot in the flame region.  HiBMs is 
telemetric thereby providing pixel mapping through object space along parallel paths.  
 
The liquid crystal tunable filter is (LCTF) 10 nm bandpass and can be tuned to any wavelength 
in the near IR between 650 nm and 1050 nm.  The filter is removable for selected wavelength 
imaging across a broader spectrum with insertion of a Filter Compensator module.   
 
The maximum data rate is supported by the direct to disk hardware in the IPSU is 30 fps at full 
resolution and 12 bit depth.  The camera can be operated at 30 frames per second with 12 bit per 
pixel dynamic range. Binning may be selected to reduce data storage requirements. Sub frame

3.0   FCF OVERVIEW 
3.1   Fluids and Combustion Facility  
The FCF is a modular, multi-user facility developed by Glenn Research Center (GRC) 
for permanent installation in the ISS US Lab Module to support technology development 
and validation in support of Space Exploration.  This facility establishes an initial 
operational capability for microgravity fluid physics and combustion science on-board 
ISS.    FCF’s  scope  started  with  design  and  progressed  through  development,  
production, deployment and operation in ISS.  
FCF consists of two powered racks and sufficient on-orbit stowage in ISS for FCF and 
payload hardware.  The two racks are the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the 
Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR).  FCF operates together with payload experiment 
equipment and ground-based operations facilities to perform fluids and combustion 
science experiments within available FCF and ISS resources. 
3.2   Combustion Integrated Rack  
The CIR is designed to support a wide variety of combustion sciences in space.  Solid, 
liquid and gas fuels are burned in a Chamber.  Diagnostics are used to capture 
important attributes of the combustion event such that scientists may better understand 
the combustion process.   
Components located in the CIR will consist of two (2) types of hardware; permanent 
facility hardware, designed to serve multiple Principal Investigators (PI), and PI-specific 
hardware, designed to be replaced as part of each experiment to be performed.  The 
CIR design is to be installed in a standard Boeing ISPR.  A folding door is used over the 
front of the assembled rack.

4.0   CIR/MDCA INTERFACE SECTION 
CIR and MDCA hardware was launched on STS 126/ULF-2from Kennedy Space Center 
in November 2008.  After delivery, CIR was installed in the United States Laboratory 
Module, and MDCA was installed into the CIR.  It is anticipated that FLEX2 hardware 
will be manifested on ATV2 or ULF5 in 2010, and will be integrated into MDCA by the 
crew after the completion of FLEX and FLEX-Helium experiments.   
4.1   MDCA/FLEX2 Experiment Overview 
4.1.1   Payload Description 
MDCA is designed to support experiments that investigate the fundamental 
combustion/suppression/extinguishment aspects of fuel droplets under different 
pressures and ambient oxygen concentrations for a range of fuel droplet sizes.  The 
MDCA/FLEX2 experiments include hardware that is based on the design of the 
MDCA/FLEX hardware, with minimal changes made to accommodate droplet array 
experiments.  The most extensive design changes are with regard to the Retractable 
Index Fiber (RIF), and the igniter tips, as will be described in section 5.  The FLEX2 
hardware that has no changes from the FLEX design consists of gas bottles, and an 
adsorber cartridge, both of which are CIR provided.  Additional needle assemblies and 
fuel reservoirs are provided by FLEX2 and are also identical to those used in FLEX.  
The fuels loaded into the reservoirs, however, will differ from those used in FLEX, as is 
discussed in section 5.      
4.1.2   Experiment objectives 
The objective of MDCA is to provide the apparatus for dispensing, deploying, and 
igniting fuel droplets while the CIR provides the diagnostics, structure, supporting 
avionics, and infrastructure for recording, processing, and downlinking the data from the 
combustion event.  The MDCA initial experiments consist of the FLEX investigations.  
FLEX utilizes pure Methanol and pure Heptane as fuels.  FLEX2 is a follow-on 
experiment planned to begin after the completion of FLEX and FLEX-Helium (He), and 
utilizes pure Ethanol and Decane fuels as well as mixtures of fuels, and provides the 
added capability of igniting arrays of fuel droplets tethered to a beaded fiber. 
4.1.3   Experiment Hardware Description 
The MDCA hardware consists of three distinct hardware components.  The Chamber 
Insert Assembly (CIA) provides the mechanisms for initiating the combustion event.  
The Avionics Package is the center of control and power distribution for the MDCA.  PI 
Specific Diagnostic Packages consist of diagnostics provided by CIR that are necessary 
to meet science requirements and are not provided by MDCA.  An example of this is the 
additional Image Processing Unit (IPSU) and High Bit Depth/Multispectral (HiBMs) 
camera that FLEX2 requires for its operations.  CIR will also be responsible for the 
negotiation of the up-mass of replacement components for MDCA hardware and 
consumable items that are supplied by CIR as specified in CIR-MDCA Integration 
Agreement (FCF-IA-MV-MDCA).  The consumable items required by FLEX2 include an 
adsorber cartridge and gas supply bottles.  The safety assessments for these CIR items

5.0   MDCA STRUCTURAL/MECHANICAL 
5.1   Chamber Insert Assembly 
The MDCA CIA (See FIGURE 3 and FIGURE 4) is a multi-functional apparatus 
designed as the major platform used for mounting integral sub-system hardware to 
perform combustion science.  The CIA consists of the Internal Apparatus, which is the 
functional hardware of the experiment, the Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS), upon 
which the Internal Apparatus is structurally based, and electrical and thermal 
interconnects.  The Internal Apparatus is capable of dispensing, deploying and igniting 
fuel droplets with small velocities relative to the field of view of the diagnostic 
equipment.  The Internal Apparatus of MDCA consists of two fuel dispensing systems, 
dual needle deployment mechanism, two hot wire igniters, an indexing fiber support 
mechanism, radiometers, pressure-sensitive igniter switch, and thermistors.   
During the mission, the crew may replace igniters, the fiber support mechanism, fuel 
reservoir, and deployment needles.

5.2   Internal Apparatus 
5.2.1   Fuel Dispensing System 
There are two fuel dispenser systems on the CIA.  Each fuel dispenser system has two 
subassemblies; the replaceable fuel reservoir assembly and the dispenser motor 
assembly.  The fuel reservoir is composed of a syringe and attached latching solenoid 
valve, an aluminum housing, and a transparent plate of Lexan F2100.  The dispenser 
motor assembly is composed of a drive screw, a stepper motor, an incremental 
encoder, and structural base.  During the software controlled dispensing sequence, fuel 
is dispensed from one syringe, through the latching solenoid valve to its own 
deployment needle.  The solenoid valve is sent a voltage pulse that switches the valve 
to its alternate state.  The syringe valve will be closed immediately following the 
dispensing of the fuel droplet.  
Two identical dispenser systems are present for improved reliability when using a single 
type of fuel.  Alternatively, each syringe may contain a mixture of fuels.  In addition, the 
entire fuel reservoir assembly may be replaced if necessary by separating the fuel line 
bayonet, the valve power connectors, and loosening the captive fasteners.  To monitor 
the temperature of the fuel, each syringe is outfitted with a thermistor. 
FLEX2 requires the use of Ethanol, Decane, and a set of fuel mixtures.  Additional 5 ml 
fuel reservoirs will be delivered in the FLEX2 cache of hardware, pre-filled with the

5.2.2   Fuel Reservoir System 
While the fuels loaded into the reservoirs differ between FLEX and FLEX2, the fuel 
reservoir design is identical.  The fuel reservoir is a gas-tight glass syringe and stainless 
steel plunger.  The plunger tip is covered by Teflon, which forms a dual wiper seal 
against the inside of the syringe.  The syringe is covered by a tygon sleeve that is 
epoxied to the syringe at its top.  The tygon-enshrouded syringe body is lightly clamped 
between a transparent cover and the housing.  The syringe feeds fuel directly to an 
attached latching solenoid valve.  It is also epoxied to the solenoid valve at its bottom.  
The fuel is fed from the valve through polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) tubing to the 
dispenser needles.  A quick disconnect in the tubing is necessary to allow removal of 
the fuel reservoir.   
Each syringe has two levels of containment.  In addition to the tygon sleeve, the syringe 
is enveloped in an aluminum sleeve that is covered by a transparent Lexan 9604 barrier 
to protect against impact.  See FIGURE 6. 
Each syringe can contain 5.0 ml of fuel.  Nearly all of the fuel in the syringe is capable of 
being dispensed.

5.2.3   Deployment System 
The FLEX2 deployment mechanism is identical to that of MDCA/FLEX, and consists of 
two replaceable deployment needles mounted on brushless servo motors and bi-stable 
brakes.  The deployment needles are flared tubes (See FIGURE 8) connected to the 
Dispenser System via .012 inch OD, .01 inch ID, PTFE tubing.  The deployment 
needles are inverted relative to each other and opposed 180 degrees as illustrated in 
FIGURE 9.  During deployment, the needles move in a plane common to the igniters 
and fiber.  Each needle is moved by a brushless servo motor, which rotates the needles 
to a pre-determined position verified by motor encoder feedback.  Just before 
dispensing fuel, the needles are positioned in close proximity to each other.  Fuel from 
each of the fuel dispenser systems is routed to its dedicated deployment needle tip to 
create a single droplet of a desired size.  Upon completion of fuel dispensing, the 
deployment motors actuate again, rotating to increase the gap between the needles and 
to minimize the needle surface contact with the droplet.  Finally, the needles are rapidly 
withdrawn simultaneously.  The rapid synchronized retraction of the needles causes the 
fuel droplet to detach from the deployment needles with little or no residual motion.  
Either deployment needle may be used to dispense the droplet via its fuel dispenser 
system.  The needles may be replaced by separating the bayonet assembly in the fuel 
line and unfastening the needle fixture on the motor axis.  Per the replacement 
procedure, which is performed at the ISS provided work bench, the deployment needles 
will be removed only after its cover has been installed.  This cover, shown in FIGURE 
10, prevents contact with the needle during removal/installation.  Each needle has its 
own cover that remains attached during stowage.  Needles will be individually bagged 
upon replacement to contain any residual fuels and broken material.

5.2.4   Ignition System 
While the MDCA/FLEX igniter tips uses two identical round heating elements with single 
loops, the FLEX2 ignition tips consist of two heating elements with a dual loop 
configuration.  The elements are Kanthal hot wire igniters mounted on removable 
ceramic mounts (See FIGURE 11).  The elements have  can simultaneously ignite a two 
bead droplet array on the retractable index fiber.  The ceramic mount is mounted to a 
bracket on the drive shaft.  Each drive shaft is driven by a rotary stepper motor and an 
enclosed drive screw.  Each hot wire igniter is positioned opposite the other.  The rotary 
stepper motor moves the igniter linearly into the deployment area to a predetermined 
position just before dispensing of the droplet.  Motor encoders automatically verify the 
igniter position.  The fuel is dispensed, the droplet is deployed, and a wait period passes 
to allow some fuel vaporization.  Then both igniters are pulsed with a brief current to 
heat the igniter and ignite the fuel vapor surrounding the droplet.  Finally, the igniters 
rapidly retract out of the field of view of the diagnostic equipment.  Each igniter may be 
replaced by pulling the ceramic mount from the bracket.  The electrical connection is 
made when the ceramic mount is plugged onto the bracket. 
The igniter tips will be stowed in bags.  The crew will be required to wear gloves while 
performing this procedure.  Additionally, during this operation, which is performed at the 
ISS provided work bench, the covers for the deployment needles will be installed to 
prevent inadvertent contact. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
FIGURE 11 FLEX AND FLEX2 IGNITER TIPS  
 
5.2.5   Fiber Support System 
The FLEX2 fiber support mechanism is based on that of MDCA/FLEX, with the addition 
of crossing fibers for tethering an array of droplets.  The FLEX2 experiments employ a 
set of 79 micron diameter, 229 mm long silicon carbon-carbide fibers with  an additional 
set of crossing fiber pairs of the same material to suspend fuel droplets in an array of 
predetermined dimension.    The main fibers are supported at both ends by the arms of 
a U-shaped bracket.  The lower portion of the U- bracket is mounted to an axle.  The 
axle is attached to a rotary stepper motor that rotates the bracket and fiber

The droplet may be deployed at various intersections of the crossing fiber pairs with the 
main fiber.  There are 3 pairs of crossing fibers with two pairs 12mm apart, and 1 pair at 
24mm apart.  They are attached by epoxy to a cross member that is attached to the U-
shaped fiber arm bracket.  A second rotary stepper motor actuates a rack and pinion 
mechanism.  The rack and pinion mechanism allows the fiber to be indexed along the 
axis of the fiber.  Deployment onto the fiber is limited to the central 129 mm of the fiber 
because using the extreme ends of the fiber would bring the bracket arms close enough 
to interfere with the combustion event.   
When a tethered droplet array is desired, one of the crossing fibers is moved into 
position, the droplet is dispensed onto the cross fiber, and the fiber is translated the 
distance of the cross fiber pair spacing.  There are two crossing fiber pairs spaced 
12mm apart, and one pair spaced 24mm apart.  The next droplet is then dispensed onto 
the second cross fiber pair.  The deployment needles retract, and the igniters ignite the 
droplets.  
The hardware-restricted spherical volume around the center of the droplet is called the 
zone of exclusion.  When the fiber is not being used, the fiber will be in the retracted 
mode, clear of the deployment area and diagnostic fields of view.  Rotational retraction 
speeds of the RIF are nominally from 2°-6°/sec. 
The fiber support mechanism may be replaced in case of damage with stowed spares 
by unfastening the captive fasteners shown in FIGURE 13.  The Fiber Arm is replaced 
at the ISS provided work bench after the CIA is removed from the chamber.  It requires 
no complicated alignment techniques and no electrical power.  Included in the Fiber 
Arm replacement procedure is the installation of the protective cover for the fiber which 
prevents inadvertent contact.  The Fiber Arm is stowed with this cover installed.  To 
prevent handling damage, each Fiber Arm Assembly is shipped with a protective cover 
(FIGURE 14).

5.2.6   Water Cooling System 
The details of the water cooling system are unchanged by the FLEX2 operations, and 
are included in the MDCA safety data package MDC-DOC-1679.  The CIA will take in 
water from the CIR Water Thermal Control System through the IRR.  CIA intake and 
exhaust lines will connect to the IRR.  The CIA water lines provide the interface 
between the CIR IRR and the MDCA CIA structure. The coolant system will connect to 
the CIR IRR with quick disconnects. 
 
5.2.7   Pressure Sensitive Igniter Switch 
The details of operation of the pressure sensitive igniter switch are unchanged by the 
FLEX2 operations, and are included in the MDCA safety data package MDC-DOC-
1679.  While the physical and electrical operation of the switch is unchanged, its role no 
longer functions as a hazard control in FLEX2.  The updated detonation analysis shows 
that the fuel to O2 mixture ratio drops below the flammability limit as pressure 
increases.  Therefore no hazard is associated with high pressure operations.      
 
6.0   MDCA ELECTRICAL/AVIONICS  
6.1   MDCA Avionics Package Hardware 
The MDCA Avionics Package is made of aluminum alloy, 6061-T6.  Some structural 
components may be composed of corrosion resistant stainless steel, A286. 
The Avionics Package is an aluminum box that provides a physical housing, an EMI 
shield, and connection to the CIR Optics Bench electrical interconnects.  The housing 
will be mounted on the Optics Bench at the Principal Investigator Location (PIL).  This 
housing has inlet and exhaust vents to interface with the CIR Air Thermal Control 
System.  The housing is illustrated in FIGURE 15 and FIGURE 16.

9.3   MDCA/FLEX2 Test Operations 
9.3.1   Number of Test Points 
FLEX2 has a test matrix with 550 points, as enumerated in Table 3 of the Science 
Requirements Document (SRD).  The test points are distributed among mixed fuel tests 
and pure fuel tests.  The pure fuel tests include the fiber droplet array tests and the flow 
velocity tests, created by the translation of the fiber during the burn event.  A preliminary 
test matrix was constructed to address these requirements, and to keep the number of 
experiments to a manageable level, resulting in 456 test points.   
9.3.2   Resource Estimates 
This section presents the preliminary estimated amount of necessary resources 
determined from the experiment science requirements and the preliminary test matrix.  
The fuel reservoirs have a 5 ml capacity, but the actual volumes are dependent on the 
results of future detonation analysis.
